title: Pre-Bill Claim Review for Behavioral Health: Claim Scrubbing vs Documentation Review
summary: A claim scrubber tells you a claim will process, not that it will survive a records request. What scrubbers check and miss, pre-bill documentation checks by BH service, a hold-and-release workflow with SLAs in hours, clinician messages that get fixed, and the metrics to track.
body_markdown:
Pre-bill claim review means checking a claim before it reaches the payer, and in behavioral health it has two halves. Claim scrubbing checks the claim itself: codes, units, modifiers, eligibility and payer edits. Documentation review checks whether the chart supports the claim: medical necessity, time, signatures, a current treatment plan, level of care and, for SUD records, Part 2 consent. BH programs need both before submission, and the second is easy to skip because no claim edit forces it.


A scrubber tells you a claim will process. It can't tell you the claim will survive a records request. This guide covers what scrubbers check and miss, the difference between a clean claim and a defensible one, what documentation review should check by service, a workflow that holds only the claims with findings, clinician messages that get fixed, metrics and where sampling fits.


The short version


- A scrubber answers "will this claim process?" Documentation review answers "will it hold up if the payer asks for the record?" Federal Medicaid rules don't even count a claim under medical necessity review as clean.
- Scrubbers check NCCI edits, eligibility, code validity, required fields and payer rules. They can't see signatures, session time, plan currency, level-of-care support or Part 2 consent.
- Hold only claims with a blocking finding, measure the hold in hours, and let everything else go out on schedule.
- Clinician messages work when they're specific, cite the rule, include a drafted fix and set a due date. Corrections go in as dated late entries, never backdated.
- OIG's General Compliance Program Guidance (November 2023) says claims audits should include clinical review of medical necessity by an appropriately credentialed clinician.


## Claim scrubbing vs documentation review


The two checks look at different evidence and fail in different ways. A scrubber failure shows up within days as a rejection or a CO-16 denial. A documentation failure can sit quietly for years, then come back as a recoupment, often extrapolated.


Claim scrubbing Pre-bill documentation review


**Question it answers** Is the claim built correctly for this payer? Does the record support every line on the claim?


**Reads** The 837 claim data, eligibility responses, code sets and edit tables Progress notes, assessments, treatment plans, signatures, orders, consents, authorizations


**Typical findings** NCCI conflict, units over the MUE, invalid code, missing NPI or modifier, inactive coverage Time doesn't support the code, unsigned note, expired plan, level of care not justified, no Part 2 consent on file


**Who fixes it** Billing staff Clinicians, supervisors, utilization review, then billing


**Cost of missing it** Rejection or denial, rework, delayed cash Overpayment demand after an ADR, prepayment review or audit


If your RCM team runs a scrubber, the first column is covered. The second column is where BH revenue integrity actually lives, because BH claims are cheap to build and expensive to defend.


## What claim scrubbers check


- **NCCI procedure-to-procedure (PTP) edits.** Code pairs that shouldn't be billed together for the same patient on the same date, unless a modifier and the documentation justify it.
- **Medically unlikely edits (MUEs).** CMS defines an MUE as the maximum units of a code reported on the vast majority of appropriately reported claims by the same provider for the same beneficiary on the same date. CMS updates the published files quarterly, and some MUE values are confidential, so no scrubber catches every one. Section 6507 of the Affordable Care Act requires state Medicaid programs to use compatible NCCI methodologies, so these edits hit Medicaid claims too.
- **Eligibility.** Active coverage on the date of service, the right plan, and coordination of benefits.
- **Code validity.** Deleted or not-yet-effective CPT, HCPCS and ICD-10-CM codes after each annual or quarterly update.
- **Required fields.** Rendering and billing NPI, taxonomy, place of service, authorization number, units. Our[CO-16 guide](https://blog.adentris.com/co-16-denial-code-behavioral-health/) covers the BH-specific misses here, including supervised clinicians and UB-04 revenue code pairing.
- **Payer-specific rules.** Frequency limits, modifier requirements and code-by-payer edits. Telehealth is a good example, because the right POS and modifier differ by payer, as our[2026 telehealth billing guide](https://blog.adentris.com/telehealth-billing-behavioral-health-2026/) shows.


All of this matters. A good scrubber pays for itself in avoided rejections. But every item on that list can be checked from claim data alone, and that's exactly its limit.


## What scrubbers miss


A scrubber has never opened a progress note. It will pass a perfectly formatted claim for a session the chart doesn't support. These are the six gaps that matter most in BH:


- **Medical necessity.** The record has to show symptoms that affect functioning and a reason this service is needed now. The First Coast psychotherapy LCD (L33252) says statements such as "supportive psychotherapy given" are not adequate.
- **Time.** Psychotherapy codes are time-based. Medicare billing article A57520 lists 16 to 37 minutes for 90832, 38 to 52 for 90834 and 53 or more for 90837. A 41-minute note billed as 90837 sails through any scrubber.
- **Signatures.** An unsigned or late-signed note is invisible to claim edits. The rules on valid signatures, timeliness and attestations are in our[signature requirements guide](https://blog.adentris.com/signature-requirements-clinical-documentation/) .
- **Plan currency.** L33252 expects treatment plans to be updated generally at least every three months. Medicare PHP needs physician recertification by day 18 and then at least every 30 days, and IOP at least every 60 days, under 42 CFR 424.24.
- **Level-of-care support.** For SUD care, the assessment has to justify the ASAM level billed, and the authorized level has to match it.
- **Part 2 consent.** A Part 2 program needs written patient consent before disclosing SUD records to a payer. Since the 2024 rule, one consent can cover all future treatment, payment and health care operations disclosures until the patient revokes it in writing (42 CFR 2.31 and 2.33). See our[Part 2 consent guide](https://blog.adentris.com/42-cfr-part-2-consent-documentation-guide/) for the required elements.


## Clean claim rate vs a defensible claim


"Clean claim" is a processing term. Federal Medicaid rules define it as a claim that can be processed without getting more information from the provider or a third party, and they explicitly exclude a claim under review for medical necessity (42 CFR 447.45). State Medicaid agencies must pay 90% of clean practitioner claims within 30 days. Nothing in that definition asks whether the chart supports the service.


A defensible claim is one that would survive a records request. It's coded to what the record shows, by an eligible clinician, under a current signed plan, with the necessity argument written down. A program can post a high clean claim rate and still fail a prepayment review, which our[prepayment review guide](https://blog.adentris.com/prepayment-review-behavioral-health/) covers in detail.


Here's a worked example. A clinician sees a client for individual therapy and the note shows 2:05 to 2:46 PM. The claim goes out as 90837. Eligibility is active, the NPI and taxonomy are right, there's no NCCI conflict, and the scrubber passes it. The clearinghouse accepts it, and the payer pays it.


Then a records request arrives. On review, the 41 documented minutes support 90834, not 90837, so the difference becomes an overpayment. Multiply that by a pattern across a clinician's caseload and you have an extrapolation problem.


## What pre-bill documentation review checks, by BH service


Service Check before billing Common failure


**Outpatient psychotherapy** Documented time matches the code. Plan in effect and signed. Specific interventions and client response. Symptoms tied to functioning. For telehealth, modality and client location Time short of the billed code. Boilerplate notes. Plan expired weeks ago


**IOP and PHP** Hours delivered match the program billed. Physician certification and recertification on time (Medicare: IOP at least 9 hours a week and recert every 60 days, PHP at least 20 hours and recert by day 18, then every 30). Plan sets type, amount, frequency and duration Attendance short of the weekly minimum. Recert missing or late. Copy-forward group notes


**Residential** ASAM level in the assessment matches the level billed and authorized. Daily documentation. Continued-stay reassessment with new information. Authorized dates cover billed days Days billed past the authorization. Reassessment copied from admission. Level not justified


**MAT and OTP** Initial psychosocial assessment and care plan within 14 days of admission, and a periodic physical exam at least yearly (42 CFR 8.12). Dosing and counseling records match billed units. For telemedicine buprenorphine, PDMP review date and time (21 CFR 1306.51). Part 2 consent covering the payer Care plan late or never updated. Counseling billed without a note. No consent covering payment disclosures


Medicaid manuals and payer contracts add their own items, and some set tighter deadlines than Medicare. Build the checklist from the rules each payer actually applies to your programs, not from a generic template.

A 24-item scorecard for 10 charts. Score a sample by hand first to see which documentation gaps are worth turning into pre-bill hold rules.

## A pre-bill workflow that doesn't stall cash


The fear with pre-bill review is a growing pile of held claims. That happens when review means a person reading every chart before release. It doesn't happen when rules run on every claim automatically and people only touch the exceptions.


1. **Hold rules.** Hold only lines with a blocking finding: no note, unsigned note, time below the billed code, expired plan or authorization, missing consent. Release everything else on the normal schedule. Advisory findings, like a thin intervention description, go to education, not to the hold queue.
2. **Queue order.** Sort held claims by timely filing date first, then dollar value. Medicare allows one calendar year from the date of service (42 CFR 424.44), and Medicaid generally 12 months. Commercial contracts set their own, sometimes shorter, limits.
3. **SLA in hours.** Measure from hold to release, not from date of service.
4. **Owner by finding type.** Route each finding straight to the person who can fix it, never through a general billing inbox.
5. **Escalation.** If the owner misses the SLA, the supervisor gets the item, then the clinical director. If a finding can't be fixed honestly, the claim is corrected or not billed.


Finding Owner Our suggested SLA Escalate to


Unsigned note or missing co-signature Clinician, then supervisor 24 hours Clinical supervisor at 24 hours


Time doesn't support the billed code Clinician confirms, billing recodes 24 hours Billing lead recodes to the documented time


Plan expired or missing signatures Primary clinician 48 hours Clinical director


Authorization or level-of-care mismatch Utilization review 48 hours UR manager and program director


Missing Part 2 consent Intake or front desk 72 hours Compliance officer


Claim data error (NPI, units, modifier) Billing Same day Billing manager


These SLAs are starting points, not a standard. Track the 90th percentile hold time, not just the average, because a few claims stuck for weeks do more damage than many held for a day. I'd rather see a claim held four hours than paid and recouped two years later.


## Clinician messages that actually get fixed


This step decides whether pre-bill review works. When clinicians get a month-end spreadsheet with no note, date or reason attached, nothing gets fixed. What works is narrow and specific:


- **One finding per message,** naming the client, date and service.
- **The rule, cited.** "Policy says" doesn't persuade anyone. A specific billing article, regulation or payer manual does.
- **A drafted fix** the clinician can approve or edit, with every option honest.
- **A due date in hours,** tied to the claim hold.
- **Delivered where they work,** inside the EHR task list or the tool they already check.


What doesn't work: batch emails, "please review your notes," findings with no rule behind them, and any message that reads like a reprimand. Repeat findings belong in a supervision conversation, not in a tenth automated reminder.


Sample message: time doesn't support the billed code


**Fix needed before billing:** individual psychotherapy, client \[initials, MRN\], \[date of service\]


**Finding.** The note documents 41 minutes (2:05 to 2:46 PM). The claim is coded 90837, which needs 53 minutes or more. 38 to 52 minutes supports 90834.


**Rule.** CPT time thresholds as applied in Medicare billing article A57520 (Psychiatric Diagnostic Evaluation and Psychotherapy Services).


**Choose one.** (1) The times are correct: approve the change to 90834 and nothing in the note changes. (2) The session ran longer and you have a basis for the actual times: add a late entry dated today that states the correct times and how you know. Do not edit the original entry.


**Due.** Today by 5:00 PM. The claim is on hold until then. Questions go to \[billing lead name\].


## Correct the record the right way


Pre-bill review creates pressure to "fix" notes, and that pressure needs a guardrail. Medicare's Program Integrity Manual, Chapter 3, section 3.3.2.5, expects services to be documented when they're rendered. Any amendment, correction or delayed entry must show its own date and author and be clearly and permanently marked as such. Reviewers judge those entries under the signature rules in section 3.3.2.4.


- Never backdate. A late entry carries today's date, its author and the reason.
- Never delete or overwrite the original text. Add to it.
- Never add detail nobody can support. If the session didn't include it, the note doesn't get it.
- When the record can't support the claim, change the claim: lower the code, drop the line, or don't bill.
- Use a signature attestation only where the rules allow it. Our signature guide covers when they're accepted.


Reviewers who spot a pattern of after-the-fact additions treat it as an authenticity question. Medicare review contractors must refer documentation with potentially fraudulent entries to a UPIC, and that's a much bigger problem than one denied claim.


## Metrics that show whether pre-bill review works


Metric How to calculate it What it tells you


**First-pass yield** Claims paid on first submission divided by claims submitted Whether claims go out right the first time


**Initial denial rate** Denied claims (or dollars) divided by claims (or dollars) adjudicated What's still getting past both checks


**Findings per 100 claims** Documentation findings divided by claims reviewed, times 100, by finding type Where documentation breaks, and whether it's falling


**Hours held** Median and 90th percentile time from hold to release Whether review is costing cash flow


**Recurrence by clinician** Same finding type for the same clinician within 30 days Who needs a template fix, training or supervision


Watch these together. Findings per 100 claims should fall over the first quarter as fixes move upstream. If they don't, the problem is probably a template, not a person.


## Sampling vs full pre-bill review


OIG's General Compliance Program Guidance, published in November 2023, tells compliance committees to schedule audits from an annual risk assessment and names medical record documentation as an area for routine monitoring. It also says that, because Medicare requires services to be reasonable and necessary, claims reviews and audits should include a medical necessity review by an appropriately credentialed clinician. OIG warns that audits without that clinical review may fail to identify important compliance concerns.


Sampling has a place in that program. It's how you validate the rules and catch judgment calls no checklist will. But a sample reviewed after billing can only find a pattern once the money is out. Full pre-bill review runs every claim through the rules a machine can test, and sends people only the findings. Our write-up on[100% chart sweeps vs sampling](https://blog.adentris.com/chart-audit-sud-full-sweep-vs-sampling/) walks through what sampling misses, so I won't repeat it here.

## Frequently asked questions


**What is the difference between claim scrubbing and pre-bill review?**


Claim scrubbing checks the claim data: codes, units, modifiers, NCCI edits, eligibility and payer rules. Pre-bill documentation review checks the chart behind the claim: medical necessity, documented time, signatures, a current treatment plan, level-of-care support and consent. Scrubbing prevents rejections and quick denials. Documentation review prevents overpayments found later in audits.


**What does a claim scrubber check?**


Most scrubbers check NCCI procedure-to-procedure edits, medically unlikely edits, eligibility, code validity, required fields such as NPI, taxonomy and place of service, and payer-specific rules such as frequency limits and modifier requirements. They work from claim data, so they can't tell whether the chart supports the service.


**What is a clean claim?**


Federal Medicaid rules define a clean claim as one that can be processed without more information from the provider or a third party, and exclude claims under medical necessity review (42 CFR 447.45). A clean claim can still be unsupported by the record, which is why clean claim rate alone doesn't measure audit risk.


**How long should pre-bill review hold a claim?**


Hours, not days. Hold only claims with a blocking finding, route each finding to the person who can fix it, and track the median and 90th percentile time from hold to release. Same-day release for claim data errors and 24 to 72 hours for documentation fixes are reasonable starting targets.


**Can a clinician fix a note after a pre-bill finding?**


Yes, with a properly labeled late entry or addendum that carries the current date, author and reason, without changing the original text. CMS expects amendments and delayed entries to be clearly and permanently identified. Backdating, or adding details that didn't happen, is never acceptable. If the note can't support the claim, change the claim.


**Does OIG expect providers to audit claims before billing?**


OIG's General Compliance Program Guidance doesn't mandate pre-bill review specifically. It expects audits scheduled from an annual risk assessment, routine monitoring of areas such as medical record documentation, and claims reviews that include a medical necessity review by an appropriately credentialed clinician. Pre-bill review is one practical way to meet that expectation.
